maintopic: AUDIBILITY OF DEBATE-REPORT OF MR. SPEAKER ON AMPLIFICATION SYSTEMS
AUDIBILITY OF DEBATE-REPORT OF MR. SPEAKER ON AMPLIFICATION SYSTEMS
speechtext:
For some time hon. members of this house, together with members of the press gallery, have complained about the difficulty in hearing speeches by hon. members who are seated some distance from them. When I was in Europe last fall I visited the seats of government in Italy, Switzerland, France and the United Kingdom, to ascertain what system of amplification was being used in the assemblies of these countries, and its effectiveness. I found in Italy, Switzerland and France that members speak from a rostrum; that is to say, the member who is speaking goes either to a central microphone or to one of several microphones in the chamber.
The installation of an amplification system under such circumstances is a relatively simple matter, but it could not be adapted to our parliament. Our system is based on
the British system, of government and opposition facing each other, where hon. members speak from their seats as and when permitted by Mr. Speaker. I was therefore particularly interested in the voice reproduction system which has been installed in the chamber of the British House of Commons. I was informed that the fundamental principle behind the system in the British house is to diffuse sound from miniature loud-speakers at a sound level not greater than that at which a listener will hear if he is within a few feet of the member who is speaking. This is accomplished by microphones suspended over the benches in the chamber and by loudspeakers placed in the backs of the benches.
There are, in all, fourteen microphones. Six of these microphones, at approximately equal intervals, are suspended from the ceiling of the chamber. These are placed just above the front benches of the government and the opposition at a height of approximately eight and a half feet above floor level. The remaining seats in the house are served by eight microphones, four on each side of the chamber, suspended into the chamber on rods which are attached to the lower part of the galleries. In addition to these microphones there is a microphone overhead in the canopy of the Speaker's chair, and also a microphone on the table. The loud-speakers are placed at the top of the backs of the members' benches, and also at the top of the backs of the benches in the galleries at intervals of about four feet. These loud-speakers are circular in shape, and are quite small, having a diameter of about three inches.
The system is controlled by an operator who is outside the chamber but has a complete view of the chamber. When a member rises to speak, he switches the microphone located nearest to the member. The loud-speakers-or, as they may more appropriately be called, the voice reproduction units-close to the member who is speaking, are muted, as here, naturally, he can be heard quite well without the need of the reproduction units. In the adjacent zone the units are partly muted, whereas all the rest reproduce at the level required.
While I was at Westminster the officials of the house very generously gave me of their time in explaining the system to me and I am especially grateful to Dr. Oscar Faber, O.B.E., the consulting engineer, and to Mr. N. Sizer,

House of Commons the assistant chief engineer of the ministry of works, for their kindness and for their patience.
Upon my return to Canada, with the consent of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier), I invited Mr. Sizer to come to Canada in order that I could get his opinion as to whether a similar system could be adapted to our chamber. Mr. Sizer, with the wholehearted approval of the British Minister of Works, came to Canada at the end of January and was here for about a week, during which time he consulted with the chief architect and the assistant chief architect and other officials of our Department of Public Works, and also with Dr. Field, of the defence research department. He also made a careful inspection of the chamber, both generally and in detail, and on a number of days was present in our chamber when the house was in session.
Before leaving Canada he was good enough to leave with me a report on his observations, in which he says, in part, that he could see no reason why a system similar to the system now in operation at Westminster would not prove as satisfactory in Canada, and that such a system could be designed on similar lines for our chamber. I also have a report from Dr. Faber, the consulting engineer, and an additional report from Mr. Sizer, which they gave me when I was in England. Mr. Sizer left with me and our departmental officials a number of photographs, together with one of the microphones and one of the loud-speakers.
May I also say that the chief architect's branch of our Department of Public Works, in conjunction with Dr. Field, of the defence research department, has considered the installation in our chamber of a low-level system similar to the one which I have described. The officials of these two departments, I am pleased to say, are very well informed on this system of amplification, and believe that it can be installed so as not to cause any objectionable features from a decorative point of view.
I am satisfied from the investigations that have been made that the only amplification system which would be generally acceptable to the members of our house is one similar to the system now in operation at Westminster. I would not want to ask members to accept my recommendation, nor would I want to assume the sole responsibility for any system that is installed. It has occurred to me that it might be advisable for the house to appoint a committee to examine in more detail the system in the British house. I would be pleased to put at the disposal of the

committee the reports, photographs and equipment which I have mentioned, together with any other information which may be available.
I trust that the information which I have obtained will be of assistance in determining the system of amplification which may be approved, and I can assure hon. members that I shall be pleased to give whatever assistance I can in this regard.

speakeroldname: Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 147, to amend the Foreign Exchange Control Act.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1953
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations on the second reading of this bill. In his speech on the resolution stage the other day the minister stated that the board was to be in the nature of a stand-by instrument for the future. I said the other day, and I repeat now, that we think it is proper to have a stand-by organization, and therefore we are not against the principle of this bill.
I should like to say at this point that we hope, and I hope, the minister will see to it, so far as he can, that this is as much as possible in the nature of a stand-by organization. Indeed, the minister has already indicated that certain relaxations are now being put in force, and we hope, and everyone must hope, that they will be proceeded with as far as possible.
The reason we are not opposed to the principle of this bill is that while at the present time, with the dollar finding its own level, there does not seem to be danger either of any undue outflow or any undue inflow of money-we seem to be in a certain equilibrium-nevertheless we live in a strange and unpredictable world, and therefore we think that a stand-by organization is justified.
I should like to make two or three observations with regard to the minister's speech; because while we approve the principle of the bill, we do not approve the principle of everything that has been done, and I should like to raise certain questions for the consideration of the house in respect to the operations of the board and of the government in the last few years.

The minister's speech the other day, which he made at considerable length, was a speech with interesting figures on trade, and interesting figures as to the inflow and outflow of United States exchange. The minister was in a very pacific mood. There was no occasion for him to be anything else, but in reading that speech I suggest nobody would believe, nobody would realize, that there had been any point of criticism really of the board at all. I wish to remind the house that there have been certain points of criticism, and I wish to say a word or two about it.
In particular the minister glossed over the change which was made last September when the dollar was allowed to find its level on the exchange markets. Nothing that the minister said would indicate that that really was a position basically different from the previous attitude of the finance authorities, and that it meant really a complete break with the attitude which they had followed up to that point.
I feel it is too much to expect the minister to take us into his confidence in this matter. The minister is a very candid man; nevertheless I think it would be too much to expect him to say what he might feel free to say if it were not for the exigencies of politics. I have taken the liberty therefore, Mr. Speaker, of composing a little speech which I think the minister might have made if he had been perfectly free, what I might call a candid speech. It is very short, sir, much shorter than the speech the minister actually made the other day; and unless he objects to the liberty I have taken in suggesting certain things he might have said, I will now deal with his speech that I have composed. I would say to the minister I hope he will accept this in good faith. I would say it is very kindly meant, as the man said when he murdered his mother-in-law.
Here are the words I have attributed to the minister. Perhaps the house will allow me to stick closely to my notes while I read:
"I propose on this occasion to set politics aside and give you a candid chronicle of the operation of the foreign exchange control board.
"In July, 1946, my predecessor, Mr. Ilsley, announced that the value of the Canadian dollar had been fixed at parity with the United States dollar, instead of at a discount of approximately ten per cent which prevailed during the war. The basis on which this decision was made proved quickly to be mistaken. It was made in the expectation that American prices after a brief rise would drop. This expectation proved to be quite wrong. Meantime, the increased value of our dollar, of course, promoted purchases

by Canada in the United States, and on the other hand drastically lessened American investment in Canada. As a result, we began to lose American exchange and in the year 1947 the rate of loss increased alarmingly. The opposition pointed this out to us but, of course, we could not pay any attention to what they said and we did nothing about it until late in the autumn of 1947. By November, however, we had lost over $1,100 million of the American exchange amounting to $1,624 million which was on hand in June, 1946, just before the change was made. This reduced our reserve so low that we were forced to take action. We could not take the sensible action of lowering the value of the dollar because that advice was given to us by the opposition and, accordingly, we resorted to a variety of legislative devices to lessen trade with the United States. We imposed special excise taxes, and a whole assortment of import restraints to keep out American goods and conserve American dollars. We also felt it necessary to borrow $300 million in the United States to protect the situation."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1953
speechtext: It is $150 million.

subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1953
speechtext:
"By these means, and with the help of increased Canadian exports to the United States, we managed to keep our heads above water and carry on through 1947, 1948 and part of 1949.
"The devaluation of the British pound in September, 1949, faced us with a new situation. We should, of course, have seized this new chance to free the dollar on current account, but it was still very difficult for us to do this. Apart from other reasons, the Prime Minister during the election had vehemently criticized this course, and moreover, it would have been accepting the advice of the opposition. Consequently we again fixed an arbitrary new price of the dollar at approximately 90 cents. It soon became clear that we had gone from one extreme to the other. In 1946 the dollar had been fixed too high, and in 1949 we fixed it at too low a rate. Happily, events moved quickly and prevented us from persisting in this mistake for years as we had done in the mistake of 1946. Before many months it became evident that the Canadian dollar was worth more than the amount we fixed. We persisted, however, in refusing to let it find its own level, until the summer of 1950 reality became too strong for us. I have to admit that the opposition had been for a long time urging us toward realism and in September, 1950, we finally had to take that course.
Foreign Exchange Control Act
"By this time, two things had happened. First of all, the investment attractions of Canada, stimulated by Alberta oil and Labrador iron and many other things, were becoming more and more obvious in the United States, and along with this there was a substantial amount of speculative money which the artificial depreciation of the dollar attracted.
"Our situation in retaining the 90 cents had been made much more difficult by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who in June 1950 gave a broad hint that the dollar might soon be raised. This, of course, stimulated speculation in the dollar and made it much more difficult to retain that rate.
"Accordingly, at the end of September when parliament had risen and we could not be criticized on the floor of the house we announced that the rates of exchange would be determined by conditions of supply and demand. We used the phrase 'hot money' which we thought would obscure the situation, put the blame on American speculators and prevent people from understanding the very plain and simple cause for the change, which was that we had made a mistake in undervaluing the dollar.
"It is unfortunate that our delay in taking this action made necessary the creation of an additional $200 million of inflated currency, and this of course, coming into competition with the existing dollars, helped to raise prices. It is also unfortunate that Canadians making purchases in the United States during this period were penalized by having to use the 90-cent dollar, when later events showed the dollar worth several cents more.
"During the three months after the dollar was allowed to find its own level, our holdings of American exchange ceased to jump up and down and remained practically level, showing the wisdom of the course we had so long resisted."

I have just a word or two more to add, because I would wish that that very excellent speech I have attributed to the minister might have a chance to do its own work. I do feel that the experience we have had will teach us a lesson. I hope it will teach us that there are certain things where there is not just enough wisdom in any human being or any group of human beings to set up their judgment against the judgment of the whole business world. And that is what we have been doing. I congratulate the minister, even though I am late in doing it, upon the wisdom which came to him last September. I hope he never loses it, because I have just a slight feeling that at the present time the dollar, if one may use a phrase which was once so familiar, is half slave and half free-and not as free as I should like.
I hope when the minister talks about a stand-by organization it is not with the idea that he is going to tamper with the operation of the market-unless in the case of an unbelievable emergency which, at the present time, happily does not exist.
I wish further to say that while we approve the principle of the bill, we sincerely hope that it may be possible to simplify the procedure. It is difficult of course, with a bill of only one section, to deal with it in the ordinary way. However upon looking through the sections of the Foreign Exchange Control Act I feel that there are some of them which, in view of the relaxations which have been made, are inapplicable.
For that and other reasons I move, seconded by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross):
That this bill be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce, with instructions that they have power to review the operations of the foreign exchange control board and to consider and report to this house upon the scope of legislation sufficient to provide for necessary foreign exchange control.
I hope the minister will take sympathetically my suggestion that that is the only means we have of trying to have this whole situation reviewed. It is with that in mind that I have offered the amendment for the consideration of the house.

not know that I would have any objection to the operations of the foreign exchange control board being examined by the banking and commerce committee, but in this case I shall have to oppose the amendment. As the house recalls, the Foreign Exchange Control Act will expire sixty days after the commencement of ' the present session. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the other evening one or two members asked me some questions about the operations of the Foreign Exchange Control Act; in particular the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton asked certain questions as to the present regulations governing travel to the United States. I stated

at that time that I was not familiar with the operations in detail. I gave the hon. member some preliminary answers and indicated that I would like to elaborate on them when we were in committee.
As I indicated at that time in reply to the questions asked by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, the regulations have recently been changed to provide that no permit is required for a resident traveller to take to the United States up to a combined total of $100 in United States and Canadian funds, that is $100 United States and nil Canadian; $75 United States and $25 Canadian, et cetera. Formerly the limit was $100, of which not more than $50 could be in United States funds.
A resident who is making trips to the United States on which he will not be taking out of Canada more than a combined total of $100 in both United States and Canadian funds may, on application to his bank, obtain for that purpose up to $100 United States during any calendar month. For trips involving larger expenditures, a traveller may obtain from his bank the necessary form H permit and up to $500 United States per trip for business travel and up to $500 United States during the calendar year for travel for other purposes.
Applications for amounts over these limits have to be referred to the foreign exchange control board by the applicant's bank, but are approved for bona fide travel expenditures in any reasonable amounts, having regard to the duration of the proposed journeys.
Under the recent change in the regulation a resident may retain in his possession United States currency which he may receive in the ordinary course or which he has bought from his bank up to a total of $100. These funds may be used on any trip to the United States where the amount taken out by the traveller is such that no form H permit is required. If a traveller needs to buy United States dollars for a trip to the United States, however, he must do so from his bank. Merchants who receive United States currency in the course of their business are not permitted to sell it to other residents but must turn it in to their banks.
The hon. member for Greenwood asked for some further details as to the procedure by which track is kept by the foreign exchange control board of exports to the United States. I shall outline the procedure.
Except in those cases where a customs export entry is not ordinarily required, for example, gifts up to $25 in value, other shipments up to $5 in value, et cetera, form B. 13-B is delivered by an exporter to the
Foreign Exchange Control Act collector of customs at the port of exit of the goods. This form is a combined customs export entry and foreign exchange control board form. Five copies are required, two of which are used for exchange control purposes. Where the terms of payment for an export are in accordance with the Foreign Exchange Control Act and regulations, the collector of customs approves the form B. 13-B and sends one copy to the exporter's bank aind one copy to the board.
A resident who receives United States dollars arising out of exports is required to offer them for sale to his bank, and, if the amount is more than $100, complete F.E.C.B. form C. This form is then matched by the bank with its copy of the form B.13-B covering the export in question and the bank forwards the matched forms to the board. These forms are in turn matched by the board with the copy of the form B.13-B which it received direct from customs.
The purpose of this procedure is, of course, to ensure that Canadian exports to the United States produce their value in United States dollars which are sold to a bank in Canada and thus made available to meet our requirements for United States dollars. A similar procedure applies to exports to other countries.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD. ETC.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe for the second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Ross (Souris), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Wright.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD. ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had been discussing the amendment and the subamendment to the wheat board act when the house adjourned at eleven o'clock last Tuesday. I now propose to complete those remarks.
Just before the adjournment on that day I had said that much more is at issue in what is now before the house than the subject matter of this motion or the amount of money that is involved in the payment that has been announced. The statement that was made in this house, and which first brought this subject before us, was by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). On Friday, March 2, 1951, he informed the house that a decision had been reached as to the amount that was to be paid to terminate the five-year wheat pool; and after referring to the agreement with the government of the United Kingdom, and the

fact that the government of the United Kingdom had made it clear that no further payment would be made by them under the agreement under consideration, he then said this, as recorded at page 833 of Hansard:
Hon. members may also have seen an announcement by the Chancellor of the Exchequer on February 20 that the United Kingdom will not draw further on the remainder of the credit of $1,250 million which was made available in May, 1946, and which expires on December 31, 1951.
The government has decided to recommend to parliament that an amount equal to the balance of the United Kingdom credit, namely, $65 million, be added to the sums now awaiting distribution in settlement of the five-year pool.
I pointed out that from the time that announcement was made nothing has been placed before the members of this house which would make it possible to determine by what process of arithmetic the figure of $65 million was arrived at. In the speech of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) as recorded in Hansard for Thursday, March 8, 1951, a number of figures were put on record which explained what the resulting payments to the farmers would be after this $65 million had been paid into the wheat pool and the ultimate distribution had been made. No explanation was given as to how the government decided that $65 million was the right figure. No explanation has yet been placed before this house to make it clear to us how we have this extraordinary coincidence or how it comes about that the figure to be paid to terminate the five-year wheat pool should happen to be precisely the figure that remained unclaimed by the government of the United Kingdom of that loan which had been made available to them. Since we have not yet received that explanation, I submit to the house that there is no possible explanation except that the government had set its mind on persuading the British government to take up the $65 million, and pay that as the amount remaining as an obligation by

Canadian Wheat Board Act them under the contract, and that this government would then be in a position to say to the farmers affected: This is all we were able to get from the government of the United Kingdom; we regret we could not get you any more, but this is the balance; and then would make the distribution accordingly. If there is some other explanation, let us have it. If there is some other place from which this $65 million figure was obtained, let us have it. If there is some other way in which the computation was made, then let us know so that the members of this house may have reason to decide whether the figure should have been a great deal more or whether it should have been this much.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) gave an argument which made it clear that, in his opinion, not one additional cent was owing under the contract. He challenged that statement when I made it the other night; but I read the Hansard record of what he had said, and it was quite clear that he was not suggesting that there was a balance owing by the government of the United Kingdom. It was something quite different. Let me refer to what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, as recorded in Hansard of March 12, 1951, at page 1172:
It was never suggested to the British government at any time-[DOT]
These are the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
-that they were in legal default under the agreement. It was pointed out, however, that the existence of dissatisfaction among wheat producers in Canada about the results of the agreement could have unfortunate consequence for future trade relationships between our two countries and that the British government might wish to reconsider their earlier decisions. My colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), made similar representations a few weeks ago. As the house knows, however, the British government did not see fit to make any further payments.
That was a perfectly legal and proper decision for them to make under the agreement. The Canadian government, while recognizing that the legal obligations of the British government under the agreement had been fulfilled, took a different view of the over-all results and decided to pay into the five-year pool the $65 million that remained under the United Kingdom loan act.
That is all that we are told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, namely that they decided to pay into the five-year pool the $65 million that remained under the United Kingdom loan act. That statement of course is not literally correct. They are not paying in the amount under the loan. They are paying in from the treasury to the pool an amount which happens to be the same figure as would have been available to the British government if they had decided to take that up for the purpose of making an additional payment of that amount on the contract which

has been referred to. That is a much different thing indeed. Therefore the Minister of Trade and Commerce has neither by suggestion nor otherwise given us any indication of how that $65 million was arrived at. On the contrary, I submit that there is no other explanation than the fact that in his case as in the other case the only relationship the $65 million has to the measure of dissatisfaction expressed by the wheat producers affected by this contract is that this was the figure in their mind which they were trying to get the British government to pay under this device they were seeking to employ.
Do not let anyone suggest that this is an interpretation not borne out by the facts. There is nothing else that the facts support at present. If there is some other explanation, then the members of this house are entitled to it; and they certainly will be entitled to it long before this $65 million figure comes up. But we are now discussing the broad question of this contract, its effect upon the western farmers and the manner in which the government has been handling their affairs.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has pointed out that this was a highly satisfactory agreement. The Minister of Agriculture has also pointed out that it was a highly satisfactory agreement if only the British government had lived up to their obligation. That is the position he has taken. A suggestion was made the other night, which I did not have the opportunity to deal with before eleven o'clock, that the Minister of Agriculture had not, in fact, left any such impression. It would have been extraordinary if the newspapers of this country, from one side to the other, had been so uniformly wrong in this particular case as they have been; because the newspapers right across this country have interpreted the words of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) as meaning that the British government had failed to live up to their contract. And the newspapers right across this country uniformly, without any regard to their political persuasion, without exception so far as I am aware, have pointed out the rather striking difference between the position taken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture in this case.
The Minister of Agriculture had no intention of leaving any other thought in the minds of the members of this house but the thought that the British government had failed to live up to their obligations. These are his words at page 1062 of Hansard, after referring to the statements of Mr. Strachey when he was in Winnipeg in 1946. He points out that Mr. Strachey had dealt

not only with the possibility of higher prices, but also lower prices; and he seeks to emphasize his own point of view that Mr. Strachey's remarks were devoted to the idea of high prices and the possibility of paying more under the "have regard to'' clause. However, he is quite capable of dealing with that in such manner as he sees fit. I am pointing out only that the Minister of Agriculture took great pains to show that the representative of the British government, who was in this country in 1946, did leave the impression that they were prepared to do certain things which the Minister of Agriculture now says they were not prepared to carry out. And then he uses these simple words, which cannot be misinterpreted, and I quote his words as recorded on page 1062 of Hansard of March 8, 1951:
The fact that the United Kingdom did not estimate correctly should not justify their refusal to pay.
These words are not in conformity with the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The Minister of Agriculture leaves no doubt that there was a refusal to pay something that he claims was owing. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says that there was nothing owing. He points out that there was dissatisfaction, and most certainly it is only natural that there should be dissatisfaction when the Minister of Agriculture has been placing the interpretation on this clause which he has placed upon it for the farmers affected by this contract; but that is something quite apart from what is owing on this contract, and therefore we have diametrically opposed statements by the two ministers.
I do wish to deal with the effect of that position taken by the Minister of Agriculture. I regret very much to hear the statements that were made in this house on Tuesday night in regard to the government of Great Britain. I am not frequently accused of being a socialist. It will be unfortunate if this becomes the central feature of a provincial election in Saskatchewan or in any other province because this is a matter which after all is the responsibility of the government of Canada, It would be one of the most unfortunate things that could happen in this country at this time when mutual good will and the utmost spirit of co-operation is of so much importance as between the nations of the commonwealth. It would be most unfortunate if an issue of this kind were carried onto the hustings in any province or in any election, whether it be provincial or federal. For that reason it is to be most earnestly hoped that the uncertainties which now exist as to which minister speaks for the government should be clarified without further delay.
There is another thing that should be clarified. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has made it abundantly clear that he does not think there is anything owing by the British under the contract. If there is nothing owing by the British under the contract, there is nothing owing by anyone else because the contract was between the British government and the Canadian government. If there is money owing, it is money owing for an entirely different reason. It is money owing: because the government has mishandled this matter and there is justification for the feeling to which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has referred, and the government therefore is trying to make good its default-That would be a sound justification. There could be no other justification.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
If that is so, let us be quite clear. Is this an attempt to reduce in some way to arithmetical terms the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he said, and I quote from page 1172 of Hansard:
It was pointed out, however, that the existence of dissatisfaction among wheat producers in Canada about the results of the agreement could have unfortunate consequence-
Then he went on at a later point to say that the government had decided to pay the $65 million that remained under the United Kingdom loan to terminate the five-year wheat pool. No suggestion then was made that this was paid as the balance owing under the contract. On the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce it could not be because the contract was fulfilled.
So far as anything that has been placed before this house is concerned

 I qualify my remarks in that way because the government knows that it has a great deal more information than we have received-on the basis of what has already been put forward the only possible explanation that we have is that the government believes that the farmers who were compelled to deliver their wheat did not receive a fair deal and that they should make a payment to compensate them for the dissatisfaction to which they have referred.
I have made it clear that there is a moral obligation in every case where the government takes over grain, agricultural production, services or anything else under compulsion. At a time when this house has just passed emergency legislation with powers so sweeping that it brings practically our whole economy under the government by order in council it is of the utmost importance that the people of this country shall have confidence that where the government takes over anything under compulsion, whether it be wheat, agricultural production, industrial production or services, there should be fair compensation for what is taken over.
Therefore, on the basis of demonstrated moral obligation-I emphasize those words "demonstrated moral obligation"-I am confident that the members of this house would support whatever payment seemed appropriate upon the basis of the evidence submitted which showed that money should be paid. How much that is the members of this house still wait to be informed.

The members of this house are not called upon to do crystal-gazing when they are asked to decide upon the payment of millions of dollars. The government did not just look into a crystal when it decided to


make the payment of $65 million. Surely the government had some other yardstick by which to gauge the thing that was to be done than simply the fact that there was $65 million which the government of the United Kingdom could still collect on a loan. We have not yet received that information.
These facts should be before us. The proposal has been made already by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) that there should be a royal commission to inquire into what amount is thought properly owing under these transactions. I submit that that is the one satisfactory way that clear and understandable evidence can be obtained as to what should be paid to meet this moral obligation, if that is the basis upon which the government is making the payment. Therefore I urge the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to agree to the appointment of a royal commission to inquire into the terms under which this payment should be made and the measure of compensation which should be paid to the wheat producers because of the loss they have sustained through the operations of the government in dealing with the wheat which was taken from them by compulsion.
Having said that, I would point out that it is important that the members know the basis upon which this is to be done. If the government is putting forward a proposition that the government should compensate agricultural and other producers for losses which they have sustained through the action of the government where their products have been taken over, then that principle should apply with equal force to all agricultural production as to other production in Canada. I repeat the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that this is not a payment under the contract. If the payment is the result of the adoption of the principle of compensating those whose products have been taken by compulsion for the losses resulting from the action of the government, then let us know that that is the principle and let us establish that as the principle in relation to everything that is taken over under compulsion, no matter what it may be.
Of course, that would apply to other agricultural producers as well, to hog producers, to cheese producers, to fruit growers and to all others who would be affected.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD. ETC.
speechtext:
And to potato growers and to others who would be affected by any action of this kind that might become necessary under the very sweeping powers which have been assumed by the government within these past few weeks. I am placing this proposal before the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) because he is the only one who can

now solve this problem. I am urging that he state on the one hand what the principle is, and, having stated that, that he inform the house that a royal commission will be appointed to inquire into the amount that should be paid under the principle put forward.
For the reason that I have now explained I do not propose to vote for the subamendment. As I said in my earlier remarks, we have nothing before us to show first of all what the principle is and, second, how the amount would be arrived at. I said earlier that the amount might be 50 cents a bushel; it might be 25 cents a bushel; it might be 10 cents a bushel. We want to know what it is, and I believe members of the house should have information as to how the figure is arrived at before they vote substantial sums to those who deserve it under any principle that may be established in this house at the instance of the government.
I would point out that this is not a figure that can be established with certainty in view of the fact that the premier of Saskatchewan, who has displayed some interest in this matter, himself has made it clear that he is not definite because he has said it might be a figure between 15 and 25 cents. By that statement he has supported my contention that this figure is not a determined figure. Therefore for that reason I do not think we would be advancing the interests of the western farmers by seeking to leave the impression that a fixed figure has been established. Therefore I propose not to support the subamendment.
Having said that, I wish to repeat once again what I said earlier. We support the principle that, where the government takes over wheat, agricultural production or anything else by compulsion, there is a moral obligation to make fair and just compensation. We want to know what that fair and just compensation is, and we have proposed the manner in which it can be done. Before leaving these remarks, Mr. Speaker, I wish to come back to the even greater issue that is before the house. This is not something to be lightly brushed off as some hon. members would brush it off. As was said in an editorial in one of the western papers a few days ago, there sometimes seems to be little use in talking about principle to this government because it does not understand principle. When ancient traditions are recalled, when principles which have been established as the basis of our parliamentary system are referred to, they are treated as though these were simply uninteresting points put forward in a debate for no other purpose than to criticize the government.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
This parliament did not always look at principles of this kind in that way. I should like to refer hon. members to an excellent book entitled "The Government of Canada" by Professor Dawson. At pages 206 and 207 there is a very clear, simple and forceful discussion of the principle of cabinet solidarity, the obligation of ministers to speak not as individuals but as members of a government, and to be answerable as members of a government for what they say. I quote these words from Dawson at page 206:
It follows that all members of a cabinet must consider the views of one another in making any important announcement or in taking a decision which might be considered as involving government policy; and this leads in practice to prior consultation and discussion in cabinet, or at least, with the prime minister. This done, if the minister secures agreement on his proposal, the cabinet will support it to a man; failing such agreement, the dissenting member must acquiesce in the rejection of his ideas or tender his resignation.
That is a long established practice. A minister may often be called upon to state his views as a member of the government when he has not an opportunity to consult either the Prime Minister or other members of the government. The obligation then is to consult them, and then either to be able to acquiesce in the result of that discussion or in the alternative to resign. That is no suggestion being brought forward today in this house for the first time in relation to this particular subject. That is a basic practice in regard to the collective responsibility of government to the house and to the people of Canada.
In addition to the other responsibilities raised by the discussion which has taken place, with the utmost seriousness and earnestness I place before the Prime Minister the proposition stated in Dawson's book on "The Government of Canada", a statement which simply reflects the tradition and the practices of many years. I ask that the conflicting position of these two ministers be reconciled, or, in the interests of the stature of the government in the minds of the people of Canada and its relationship with Great Britain, that a reconciliation be effected or the ordinary course be followed.

Mr. Speaker, I am not rising at this time to agree to the suggestion that a royal commission should be appointed nor to discuss any prospective provincial election in Saskatchewan or elsewhere. Nor am I speaking for effect in any other kind of election to those who have been called the hog growers, potato growers, cheese producers or any other kind of producer. Nor am I rising to quarrel with the citation from Professor Dawson that the leader of the opposition
1282	HOUSE OF
Canadian Wheat Board Act (Mr. Drew) has made. However, the leader of the opposition stated on Tuesday evening, as recorded on pages 1228 and 1229 of Hansard:
* . . with the divergence of opinion between his two senior ministers, the Prime Minister should tell us exactly what the principle is under which the payment is being made . . .
I intend to reply very briefly, first about this alleged divergence of opinion which is now referred to as a conflicting position in the government, and then about the principle under which the payment is being recommended. Obviously in any government under a parliamentary system all ministers-and I am not speaking of this government in particular-do not necessarily always have the same thoughts, nor do they necessarily always use the same expressions in communicating their thoughts. There are many matters of interest to human beings about which they do not always have the same views. If it were otherwise it would be very much simpler to have a one-man government. Our system is cabinet government, and cabinet government involves cabinet responsibility and cabinet solidarity. As I understand it cabinet solidarity requires agreement on policies and on conclusions. With respect to this "have regard to" clause, all the members of the government are agreed on the four essential points, and they are the only points which affect policy and conclusions.
The first point is that the United Kingdom had discharged all its legal obligations under the wheat agreement. Everyone recognized that was a binding contract for two years at $1.55 per bushel, and it was a contract which bound the United Kingdom government to take the number of bushels stipulated in the third and following year at a price to be agreed upon, which would not be less than $1.25 for the third year and $1 for the fourth year. That was all there was in the agreement as a binding agreement on the parties. There was a statement that in fixing the prices, which would not be less than $1.25 in the third year, the United Kingdom government would have regard to the price that was paid as the agreed price for the two first years; and that in fixing the price for the fourth year they would have regard to the price that was paid during the first year; the price for the fourth year being not less than $1. There was no obligation on them other than the undertaking to take the stipulated quantity in the third year at a price which they did not have to agree would be more than $1.25, and to take the agreed quantity in the fourth year at a price which they did not have to agree would be more than $1. No one contended there was any other legal obligation.


The second point on which there was agreement was that, at the end of May, 1950, the Canadian government accepted as the decision of the United Kingdom government that they had discharged all their legal obligations under that contract. The third point was that the Canadian wheat growers believed there was a continuing obligation under the "have regard to" clause which had not been discharged in full and that, in the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in the speech referred to by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), "the British government itself was partly to blame" for this expectation of the wheat producers because of the speech that had been made in Winnipeg by the Right Hon. Mr. Strachey, after he had listened from the galleries of this House of Commons to a speech delivered by the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Bracken.
Now, we all felt the Canadian wheat growers had understandable grounds for this expectation that there would be more done under the "have regard to" clause than had been done, and our government hoped- again I use the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the speech referred to by the leader of the opposition-"that the British government could have seen the advantage to them of making some further payments to the Canadian wheat growers." On that third point we were all agreed.
The fourth point upon which we were agreed was that the Canadian government should make a contribution to the five-year pool because producers had been led, both by United Kingdom ministers and by Canadian ministers, to expect that something more substantial would be done under the "have regard to" clause than had been done, and because the government of the United Kingdom had not seen fit to do anything more under that clause. I repeat that all the members of the government are agreed on these four points, and these are the only points about which there is any matter of policy or any matter of conclusion.

I think the hon. member will agree with me that the wheat growers of the western provinces expected from that statement, and from similar statements made by our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and by our minister of trade and commerce at that time, Mr. MacKinnon, that there would be substantial consideration resulting from the obligation of the "have regard to" clause. It was on their assumption that there was going to be something substantial coming to them as a consequence of the "have regard to" clause that they went happily along during those years, seeing to it that the wheat contract was carried out.
There is no doubt that when the government of the United Kingdom took the position that all obligations, in the sense of obligations, had been fulfilled, and that nothing more was to be done by them as a consequence of the "have regard to" clause, those expectations were not met. I think that is indisputable. We were all agreed we were not alone responsible for those expectations in the minds of the wheat producers of the western provinces. Because of the principle of solidarity invoked by the leader of the opposition, and because of the declarations that had been made by the Minister of Agriculture, by the then minister of trade and commerce and by the right hon. gentlemen from the United Kingdom, we all felt that those having such expectations should not remain in the disappointed state in which they were left by the position taken by the government of the United Kingdom that it would make no further payment as a consequence of the "have regard to" clause.
Hon. members recall that when the price for the third year was being discussed it was expressly agreed that a price of $2 would be paid for that crop, and that the matter of giving consideration to the "have regard to" clause would be postponed, When the price for the fourth year crop was again fixed at $2 it was agreed that consideration of what should be done under the "have regard to" clause would be still further postponed. It was not until the matter was raised by the representatives of the British government when the present Minister of Trade and Commerce
Canadian Wheat Board Act was in London in May of 1950 that the matter came to a head. The position they then took was that they had fulfilled' all obligations under the contract. We felt that they had fulfilled all legal obligations, but that they had not met the expectations that had been raised by the declarations made in 1946 in respect of the effect this "have regard to" clause would have on the amounts put into the pool. We came to the conclusion that the government of the United Kingdom having decided that it would do no more, we would recommend to parliament that the sum of $65 million would be put into the pool to be added to what was left there for distribution as a final payment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD. ETC.
speechtext: Why $65 million?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD. ETC.
speechtext:
Now, why $65 million? From the start it had been clearly understood there could not be any mathematical calculation of the consequence of this "have regard to" clause. I remind hon. members of the statement made by the then prime minister when the price was set for the third year of the contract; I refer to the public statement that was made at that time. He said:
Having in mind the magnitude of the agreement and the long-term security which it provides, a precise arithmetical calculation of the difference in price was not suggested.
That has been the position from the start, that there could not be any mathematical calculation of something expressed in the terms used in this agreement.
When this decision was made and accepted by the government of Canada as being the position taken, and the position they were entitled to take, in the United Kingdom, there was still $65 million that had not been drawn from the credit provided by the agreed loan of $1,250 million. Had the government of the United Kingdom seen fit to draw that amount of $65 million and use it as a settlement of anything legitimately or properly expected under the "have regard to" clause, the government of Canada would not have felt required to do anything more, and would have been quite content to say that everything that could reasonably be expected as a consequence of the "have regard to" clause had been discharged by that payment.
I am not going to repeat the argument made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that the price which in fact was paid for the fourth year crop would have provided a sum of $35 million had there not been, in the course of that crop year, devaluation of the Canadian dollar in terms of the American dollar. The government of the United Kingdom declared that it was not going to use any more of the undrawn
1284	HOUSE OF
Canadian Wheat Board Act portion of the $1,250 million loan which they were entitled to draw at any time up to December 31, 1951, and which, had they seen fit to draw it and use it for other purposes, would have required the delivery of $65 million worth of Canadian production in this year 1951. They decided that they were not going to draw anything more or put any burden on Canadian production as a resuit of any drawings under that credit.
Without attempting to make any mathematical calculation, but taking a rough approximation of what could be regarded as just and fair, the Canadian government decided to recommend to parliament that a sum equal to the $65 million be put into the pool because that placed no heavier burden on the production of this year than would have been placed upon it by the drawing and use for other purposes of the available $65 million of the credit. There was no other calculation made or attempted.
On all these points there was agreement.
It seems to me that it is not going to make much difference to the producer in western Canada what I, or the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) may think it would have been desirable for the United Kingdom to have done because of the expectations that had been raised in 1946 and that had continued as a result of the postponing of consideration of what should be done about the "have regard to" clause right up to the time the contract had been completely fulfilled. It is not going to matter much to them whether I think we should have done it or whether I think that the government of the United Kingdom should have done it. It is not going to matter much to them whether, it being done by us, it is limited to that amount or whether, in their opinion, it should be more, or whether in the opinion of someone who does not derive any benefit it should be less. On the facts we in the government are agreed. On the policy we are agreed. On the recommendation we make to parliament we are agreed. On the question of one's personal opinion of how each party has behaved, not under a contractual, enforceable obligation but under a set of expectations raised by declarations made by cabinet ministers, we are not going to have much effect upon the thinking of those who are interested as producers or those who are interested as taxpayers.
I do not think there is going to be much cheering anywhere over this decision. But I think it is the kind of decision that no one can say is an unfair and unreasonable one to make under all the circumstances which have now been quite fully discussed.

When Mr. Attlee was here I ventured to mention it to him, telling him that I was not making any request on behalf of our government that the United Kingdom do anything more, but that I felt it would not be fair for them not to know what the situation was. I suggested that if he had no objection I would raise it again with the chancellor of the exchequer when I went over for the prime ministers' conference in January; and I did so. But at no time did I suggest that there was any legal obligation, and at no time did I suggest that we had not accepted as their position the one they took in May of 1950. But I did suggest to them that they should consider whether or not in their own interest it would be wise to do something more about the "have regard to" clause, and I put the facts, as they had been placed before the members of this house, before them. Shortly after my return I was informed that they had considered my representations and had come to the conclusion that they were not going to re-open the matter.
Thereupon there was a suggestion that the right hon. Minister of Agriculture himself go over and see if he would not be able to persuade them that it would be in their interest to do something more. While it was suggested to my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and to me, that that might be some reflection on us because we had both discussed the matter, we both said that we were not sensitive on that point, and that if the Minister of Agriculture could bring about any other decision we would rejoice with him in that other decision.
Now, when he returned and told us that it was useless we said, there is nothing more we can do that will have any possibility whatsoever of getting anything further done by the government of the United Kingdom, and we have to decide whether or not in these circumstances there is responsibility upon us to do anything; and we decided-and we come before parliament agreed upon that policy and conclusion-to recommend to parliament this contribution of $65 million to be added to the price of the 1,400 million odd bushels of wheat put into the pool in the five years to which it applied.

speechtext:
In rising to
take part in this debate which has already been very well covered from every angle, I would like to deal with three things: first, the wheat agreement; does the United Kingdom owe the Canadian farmer anything, and does the Canadian government owe the farmer?
When the wheat agreement was before the house in August 1946 I supported that agreement; so did the whole of this group, and I can remember there was a great deal of criticism owing to the fact that the floor prices for wheat the last two years in the agreement were to be $1.25 for the third year, and $1.00 for the fourth year, and at that time it was brought to the attention of the house that we expected the government would maintain prices at their then levels. But even then there were signs of inflation, as far as the farmer was concerned, when he went to purchase anything.
It can be noted too that while most people expected wheat to go down on the world market, it steadily increased. When the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the leader of this group, was talking about allowing prices to rise for the things the farmer had to buy, the Minister of Agriculture rose and stated that if, at the end of the agreement, it proved to be necessary, the government of Canada could appropriate funds to compensate the wheat farmers, just as the government had already appropriated $200 million for the protection of the prices of other farm products.
Now to me that was an assurance from the minister that, should the cost of production of wheat continue to rise, some compensatory adjustment would be made by this government, but not necessarily by the British government.
We in this group have always supported the wheat board, not that we think it is perfect, but we are satisfied at this time that they are in no way to blame for this situation. The majority of the farmers today believe in the wheat board in the marketing of our wheat.
We now arrive at the question: Does the United Kingdom owe us anything on the agreement that was made? This group has never argued, as the grain trade and the Conservative party have argued, that the British government under the "have regard to" clause owed a sum equal to the difference between the price of class II wheat and the price paid under the four-year contract. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), in his statement made in the house in this debate, agrees with this position. I am convinced I have the support of this group in the contention that had there not been a
British contract class II wheat would probably not have reached the price it did. We should also remember that had all this wheat been thrown on a speculative market the farmers would not have received the price they did.
I think the statement the Minister of Trade and Commerce made in the house was a good, sound argument that the British government had met their obligations. He said the British took the position that they had fulfilled their obligations, and I gathered from the minister's statement that in his opinion this was true.
I understand the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when in England discussed the matter. He has stated so recently. Last month the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) flew to London also, and the Prime Minister has since made a statement in which he said:
The United Kingdom authorities took the position in May of 1950 "that all obligations under the 'have regard to' clause might be considered to have been taken care of." The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that this was a matter which could only be settled by the Canadian cabinet on his return to Ottawa. After discussion with his colleagues, the Minister of Trade and Commerce advised the chancellor of the exchequer of the United Kingdom that the Canadian government was in accord with the conclusions in the agreed record of the meeting held with the United Kingdom authorities while he was in London. That is one of the documents for which their consent to table has been requested. In other words, the Canadian government accepted as the position of the United Kingdom that they had discharged their obligations under the agreement.
I feel sure that this statement clears up the United Kingdom position. The United Kingdom dees not owe a further payment because, as the Prime Minister has said, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, on his return from the United' Kingdom, after discussion with his colleagues, agreed that the United Kingdom had discharged their obligations under the agreement.
Now let us look at whether the Canadian government owes the farmer anything. As long as I have been connected with the farm movement in Manitoba, the greatest desire of any farmer has been to have stability; but it was not good enough to stabilize wheat prices and then allow the cost of production to shoot higher and higher. This is one of the main grievances of the western farmer today.
The government broke faith with the western farmer. It set the price of wheat for five years, and it allowed farmers' costs to keep rising. Other agricultural producers had their prices set also; but their prices were reviewed every year and they had an opportunity of making representations to the government that their cost of production should be considered or changed.

Another very serious point with the western farmer is that from March 1, 1945, to February 17, 1947, he was compelled to subsidize the Canadian consumer by providing wheat at $1.25 to enable the consumer to get cheaper flour, hence cheaper bread. Canadian consumers, during that period of 1945 to 1947, were supplied with 160 million bushels of wheat at $1.25 when the price received under the British contract was $1.55. This, according to the figures which have been brought out in the house, would amount to approximately $48 million.
I should like to quote at this point from the Manitoba Co-Operator of March 8, 1951, at which point I find they have set out clearly what I have been attempting to say. It is as follows:
As far as the taxpayers are concerned they owed the wheat producers a very minimum of $48 million because of the fact the government mistakenly and arbitrarily imposed on the wheat producers a subsidy of this kind by requiring wheat to be sold to the mills during the period March 1, 1945, to February 17, 1947, at $1.25 a bushel, when all other buyers were paying $1.55, and sometimes more. This amounted to approximately $48 million and very definitely constituted a subsidy from the wheat grower to the Canadian consumer, reflected in the price of his bread. The difference between $48 million and the $65 million now made available is $17 million which amounts to about 11 cents a bushel on the total amount of wheat involved.
These are some of the reasons why farmers in western Canada are entitled to a payment of more than 8.3 cents.
The government failed to maintain prices. They allowed prices to go away up while we had the assurance of the Minister of Agriculture that the producer was protected under the wheat board act, just as other producers were protected under the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
In summing up I would say that the wheat agreement served a good purpose. The farmer has always asked and continues to ask for stability. The United Kingdom does not owe us anything. They have carried out their part of the bargain. And last of all 8-3 cents will not compensate the farmer for the contribution he has made to the consumer by supplying wheat at $1.25 when the world price was closer to $2.

Most farmers in the three prairie provinces have been concerned with the final payment made in the five-year pool. In northern Alberta we had drought conditions this year. Throughout the prairie provinces there was early frost and bad harvesting weather, with the result that much of the crop has not been threshed. Owing to these conditions the position occupied by the farmers has been aggravated. For that reason the farmer was concerned about what amount he would receive by way of final payment. Following the announcement by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that in addition to the $55 million in the hands of the wheat board a further contribution of $65 million would be made, totalling 8-3 cents per bushel, I have received a considerable number of wires from my constituency, especially from locals of the farmers' union of Alberta and from individual farmers, indicating a feeling that more should be paid by way of final payment.

The statement I made was to the effect that, taking into account what we did for Great Britain in supplying her with cheap wheat, the socialist government in Great Britain failed to carry out its moral obligations. Perhaps the term "moral obligation" is not a very happy term. May I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that taking into consideration what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said on the floor of this house a few nights ago, there is nothing inconsistent with what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) told us this afternoon and what he told this house on March 8, 1951, as reported in Hansard at page 1023:

Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to point out that Canada is a member of the British commonwealth of nations, the finest and greatest organization the world- has ever seen. Everything should be done to see that the relationship between the members of the commonwealth, and especially between Canada and the United Kingdom, is always a happy one. I also agree with what has been stated by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) the other night, when he said that those people who know something about the history of the British people know that they have a reputation for discharging their obligations and that their word is their bond. Just before proceeding, I should like to leave one question with him. He asked how the Canadian people were going to bear the burden of the additional costs which might be involved if the Canadian farmers were to be paid those sums to which they were justly entitled. I would ask him to ponder upon this question. If 14 million Canadian people cannot bear the burden, how does he expect 230,000 western Canadian farmers to bear the burden?

I am particularly pleased, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member has now obviously come to the conclusion that the orthodox methods of finance probably cannot meet the problem and is wanting to know how social credit would do it effectively and successfully. We have indicated that to him on many occasions. It is not our fault if he cannot understand it.
Before six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, it was insinuated that the Social Credit members

of this house had considered the Canada-United Kingdom wheat agreement to be a bad agreement. I should like to know where there exists any evidence whatsoever to substantiate such a fantastic declaration as that. It was also insinuated before six o'clock that we had, if not by direct statement at least by implication, opposed the marketing of wheat through the Canadian wheat board. There does not exist any evidence anywhere to substantiate such an assertion as that. Of course I realize that if persons are determined to do it, they can probably take statements and misconstrue such statements in order to arrive at a predetermined conclusion which would satisfy the individual but certainly could not in any way reflect the facts of the situation.
One can examine the evidence as far back as 1946, if he likes, to find the truth of our position. I sometimes regret that some hon. members of parliament are so extremely busy that they have not time to scan the records and secure the evidence. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, it makes no difference how deep one may go into any political garbage pail; one could not find evidence to back up those two assertions, that we opposed either the Canada-United Kingdom wheat agreement or the marketing of wheat through the Canadian wheat board.
As I say, everyone who will examine the records back in 1946 and 1947 will find declarations such as the one to which I am going to refer. This has been placed upon the record before, but obviously it must be placed upon the record again. In 1946 the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), referring to the Canada-United Kingdom wheat agreement, stated in part as follows, as reported at page 4800 of Hansard of that year:
On behalf of this group I wish to say that we are glad to know that we are to have stabilized prices for the next four crop years and also that an agreement has been made with Britain. I am not going to say whether we are well satisfied with the prices received. We feel that the British government are satisfied that they got a very good deal at the expense of Canada.
Then he refers to some press clippings from Britain to bear out that fact, and goes on to say:
I am glad the people of Britain appreciate that they are getting a good deal from Canada. I might say we have no objection whatever to Canada's supplying the best food in the world to Britain and to other countries, but we object to the farmers bearing the brunt of the expense. On many occasions we have made it clear that .the farmers of Canada have not received the price for their products to which they are justly entitled. I still estimate that the same condition continues under the present agreement. Of course we are very well satisfied to have a stabilized price for some time to come, because we all remember what happened

after the first great war and we do not want conditions of that kind to arise again; but in view of the losses the farmers accepted from 1939 up to 1942 I feel we are entitled to a much better deal as far as our wheat is concerned. I am not going to deal in particular with the sale to the British government. The cost of that will, of course, be taken care of by the government here, and we in turn will have to bear our share of the loss through taxation.
You will notice that on that occasion the hon. member for Battle River said what we have said repeatedly, namely that if any losses should accrue to the Canadian wheat farmers under the British agreement, then those wheat farmers should not be called upon to meet the burden of those losses by themselves. During those years we took the position that we fully recognized Britain's contribution to the democratic effort. We were anxious that Britain should have cheap wheat. We were anxious that Canadian wheat should be made available to the British people at even less than prevailing world prices. But on that occasion we emphasized that the people of every part of Canada, who all through those years kept talking about our gift to Britain, should unite in compensating the wheat farmers for any loss that might be sustained. During those years the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) spoke on a number of occasions when these matters were up for discussion. On February 27, 1947, he said;
In the early part of this agreement the farmer is making a considerable sacrifice. He is losing anywhere from 50 cents to 75 cents a bushel. If in the next two or three years there is a wheat shortage, if crops are poor, the price of wheat will be maintained at probably a high level and will remain there. Then the guarantee becomes absolutely useless. If that should be the situation over the next two or three years the farmers of this country, as a result of this agreement, are going to lose several hundred million dollars. I believe that the wheat agreement with Britain was fully justified, but it does entail in its early stages a considerable sacrifice on the part of our farmers. We feel that the sacrifice should be borne by the people of Canada as a whole.
We repeated that position time and again; and I hope that when it is referred to in this house, either during this debate or later on, hon. members will at least make an effort to stay close to the facts as they relate to our position. On March 2, when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made his announcement with respect to the $65 million and the final payment of 8-3 cents per bushel, the people of this country, particularly the farmers and farm organizations, were stunned. As a matter of fact a good many members of this house scattered through all four parties here were also stunned. I have no doubt about that whatever. I will recall the applause when the statement was commenced, but I did not hear very much enthusiastic applause at the conclusion of the
Canadian Wheat Board Act statement. As a matter of fact I thought the Prime Minister was extremely wise in offering a word of caution when the applause commenced very shortly after he started his statement.
There is a great deal of consternation among people across western Canada. We have had that feeling reflected through individual members of this house, some speaking in this chamber and others in the corridors. I would vouchsafe that if we were not assembled here; if it were not a matter of party; if it were not a matter of a government and an opposition and we were asked to express our views individually, they might be considerably different than if expressed under circumstances as they exist.
