I do not; but I am going to read the hon. member's, to see if I can learn something about my hon. friend, who has caused me a great deal of wonder on more than one occasion. We have had public statements from responsible leaders of farm organizations, men who know the facts. We have had statements from the premiers of the three prairie provinces. Certainly they are not all of the same political persuasion; in fact no two of them belong to the same party, and to me that means something. Those men know the facts as they exist now and as they have existed down through the years. We have had editorials in the western newspapers, not all favourable to a further payment, I grant you, but reflecting a weighty body of editorial opinion that the western farmers are entitled to a far better deal than they have been offered up to the present time. I daresay every member of this house who comes from western Canada has received letters, telegrams and even petitions. You know what they say as well as I do. In addition we have had the action of at least one provincial legislative assembly, that of Alberta. Perhaps others have taken action by this time; I do not know. For a moment I should like to refer to what was done in Alberta. Let us not forget that there are 56 members of the Alberta house, with one vacancy, making a total of 57. This matter

Canadian Wheat Board Act came up in the provincial assembly, and the following motion was moved by one of the members:
Whereas the Canadian government sold wheat for domestic market at a very low price during a portion of the five-year pool, and
Whereas the British wheat agreement of 1945-49 between the government of Canada and Great Britain supplied wheat to the British people at prices below those prevailing on the general world market, and
Whereas the cost of supplying Canadian wheat to the British people and the domestic market has thus far been borne entirely by the western wheat producing farmer rather than by the people of Canada as a whole,
Therefore be it resolved that this legislative assembly request the government of Canada to issue a further substantial payment to western wheat producers on all wheat delivered in' the crop years 1945 to 1949 inclusive in order to bring the total price to be received by the fanners more in line with the existing world wheat prices during the 1945-1949 period.
There are two Liberals in the Alberta house, due to the rather peculiar or different system of voting in Edmonton and Calgary, each of which returned one Liberal member. There are two C.C.F. members, and a couple of independents. During the debate on this resolution the Liberal leader in Alberta and Mr. MacDonald, the other Liberal member, tried to do a most peculiar thing. They tried to support the present position of the federal government and satisfy the farmers of Alberta at one and the same time. The press men report, at least, that they were convinced the two Liberal members were opposed to the resolution. As a matter of fact I saw an interesting report in the Calgary Albertan, a morning paper published in Calgary, referring to what took place the day of the vote. After making reference to oil, the report goes on to say:
Oil or no oil, Alberta legislators still spend a lot of time worrying about what the farmer is worrying about, and a good opportunity to worry out loud was provided in the resolution moved by Peter Chaba of Redwater, which asked for a federal payment on 1945-49 wheat deliveries in addition to the recent one of eight and one-third cents a bushel.
The only effective way to worry about the farmer, politically speaking, is out loud, because there is no point in it unless the farmer knows you are doing it. He can't tell by watching the legislator's facial expression from the gallery, because his worried look may be due only to the fact that his wife is threatening to leave him.
Anyway, the subject of wheat was shovelled back and forth for practically all of the afternoon and in some cases ground into very fine flour.
When all the chaff and dust had blown away, however, they were all in their seats, and what brought them back was a demand from the Social Credit benches for a recorded vote.
The result was surprising. Every M.LA. was on his feet for the ayes, and every one in his seat for the nays.
The surprise came to the press gallery because they could have sworn they had heard some nay

voices in the earlier voice vote, and they could have sworn that the tenor of both Liberal speeches was against the resolution.

When anyone talks about playing politics with an issue, I would refer them to that report. All members who were present voted for a resolution which asked for a payment substantially larger than 8-3 cents announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on March 2. I suggest that Alberta Liberals in the House of Commons upon this occasion should take their direction or lead from Mr. Prowse. I am the first to congratulate him when he is right-and of course I do not have to do it often. However I say he was right in the way he voted; and it would certainly be the better part of wisdom for the Liberals from Alberta in this house to follow Mr. Prowse's lead.
Figures placed on record by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) indicate that between 1946 and 1950 under the Canadian-United Kingdom wheat agreement there were losses to the tune of $431,676,844. Then, in subsidizing the Canadian consumer there was another loss of $136,920,921. In the past we have taken, and we take again today, the firm position that the Canadian people as a whole are morally obligated to make good the losses of more than $400 million sustained by the wheat farmers of western Canada, even after this 8-3 cents has been paid.
There has been divided opinion; I appreciate that. There are some who say that Great Britain should have done more under the "have regard to" clause. There are those who say that she has met all the conditions under the contract and is under no legal or other obligation to make any further payment. Some say the Canadian government should make the additional payment, and some say it should not.
The wheat farmers, who were anxious to see Great Britain get cheap bread, who were actually prepared to share the loss with the Canadian people-those farmers who were definitely led to believe that they were to be compensated for losses feel that unless those losses have been met there has been a double cross. Whether those farmers were led to believe, rightly or wrongly, that they should expect a further payment is beside the point. They were definitely given to understand that was the situation that would prevail. There is no question in the minds of the

farmers in my section of Canada as to whether the government should or should not make a further substantial payment. The twenty-five cents called for in the subamendment, even when added to the eight point three cents, is definitely lower than the total loss sustained. So in supporting the amendment which asks for twenty-five cents I feel I am asking for less than that to which the farmers are entitled. However, I am prepared to support the twenty-five cent provision, because I believe it would go a long way toward providing compensation for the loss they suffered.

Mr. Speaker, before going on with what I propose to discuss tonight, may I assert once more, so that the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) will have one more chance to find out what Social Crediters have stood for, that I and all Social Crediters supported the agreement in 1946, and we have done so ever since. We also have supported the wheat board. We believe that the agreement was a good one. We have always believed that it was a good one. We now believe that the agreement was a good one, and that the principle underlying it was also good.
What I intend to say from here on consists of my own views in large measure and not necessarily the views of every member, or even the majority of members, of the Social Credit party.
In order to start us out on the line of thought to which I wish to direct attention, may I read once more the reckless statement of the hon. member for Vegreville as it was recorded by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) at page 1097 of Hansard. It is as follows:
John Decore (Liberal-Vegreville) charged that the British government "has failed to carry out its moral obligations" to western Canada under the "have regard to" clause of the contract . . .
Had the British government assumed its obligation the farmer would have received substantially more and to which he is entitled.
May I give some attention for a few minutes to the question of the obligation of Great Britain under the contract. According to the letter of the agreement Great Britain could not be held responsible for any additional payment under the "have regard to" clause. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), as well as a good many other members, dealt with that, so I think there is no need for further discussion on it.
Now we come to the question of moral responsibility. Great Britain, according to the spirit and intent of the agreement, could not fairly and justly be held morally obligated to make any additional payment beyond the $1.55 per bushel for the first two years and $2 for the second two years of the agreement.


The Canadian government positively declared itself in favour of selling wheat to former allies at less than prevailing world prices. This is an important thing for all members to get fixed in their minds. Canada announced it as a settled policy that she was ready to sell wheat at a lower rate, not more than $1.55 per bushel, to Britain and her allies and overseas countries.
Let us see what evidence we have in connection with it. On September 19, 1945, the Hon. J. A. MacKinnon, then minister of trade and commerce, said at page 290 of Hansard:
There is a moral obligation not to take advantage of our recent allies in their time of compelling need.
On the same page the same minister said:
Higher wheat prices would encourage the importing countries in a hurried return to wheat production and pre-war wheat policies very directly to the detriment of the wheat exporting countries, particularly Canada.
Mr. Speaker, may I speak to all the members of the Liberal party who are so ready to say that Britain has not discharged her moral responsibilities? There are two definite principles laid down in 1945, apparently before there was ever any thought of a United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement. Surely no one will hold Britain accountable for those two principles!
As further evidence that the Canadian government had resolved in this direction, let me point out that the Canadian government had officially enunciated the principles laid down by the minister of trade and commerce in those two quotations I have given, by order in council P. C. 6122 passed on September 19, 1945, dealing with the proposed wheat policy for the future. I shall read the order in council. It is as follows:
Order in council directing the Canadian wheat board not to sell wheat for export to overseas destinations at a price in excess of $1.55 per bushel.

At the Government House at Ottawa Wednesday, the 19th day of September, 1945 Present:
His Excellency
The Governor General in Council:
Whereas the Minister of Trade and Commerce reports that because of the effects of a crop failure in Australia and French North Africa, of transportation difficulties in various supplying countries, and of other adverse developments upon the volume of exportable wheat and because of the urgent requirements of recently liberated areas of Europe and Asia, world demand for wheat is presently exceeding available supplies;
That under these conditions Canada, as the principal wheat exporting country, is in a position to demand very much higher prices for wheat from importing countries which must obtain food from abroad regardless of price in order to avoid want

and starvation and to many of which Canada has been or will be extending loans for rehabilitation and reconstruction purposes;
That it would be contrary to the interests of Canada and of Canadian wheat growers to take advantage of the necessity of former allies by charging higher prices for wheat, thereby encouraging an uneconomic expansion of wheat acreage in both importing and exporting countries, including Canada;
That it is in the interests of Canada and Canadian wheat growers to continue to offer wheat for sale at prices not in excess of those prevailing at the end of hostilities towards the end of maintaining a balanced agricultural program at home, securing and holding markets for Canadian wheat throughout the world and assisting in the early stabilization of economic and political life in war-torn countries;
That since May 15, 1945, the Canadian wheat board has been selling wheat to countries not in receipt of mutual aid on the basis of $1.55 per bushel for No. 1 Manitoba Northern, in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver;
That as a further means of stabilizing wheat prices during the post-war period it is the intention that steps shall be taken to ensure that producers will not at any time up to July 31, 1950, receive less than $1 per bushel for No. 1 Manitoba Northern wheat, basis in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver, on the authorized deliveries for each crop year;
And whereas by reason of the state of war now existing, it is deemed necessary for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada that the following regulation be made:
Therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and under and by virtue of the War Measures Act, is pleased to make and doth hereby make the following regulation,-
Regulation
The Canadian wheat board shall not sell wheat for export to overseas destinations at a price in excess of $1.55 per bushel for No. 1 Manitoba Northern, basis in store, Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver, and in the case of each other grade of wheat at prices in excess of such prices as in the opinion of the said board brings each of such grades into proper price relationship with No. 1 Manitoba Northern.
A. D. P. Heeney,
Clerk of the Privy Council I suppose, Mr. Speaker, everyone who is following this controversy at all must realize that the British were in no conceivable way responsible for that decision of the Canadian government to sell wheat at a price not in excess of $1.55 per bushel. When w begin to consider the moral obligation of Great Britain, this is an extremely important consideration.
We must have sold wheat to several nonBritish countries at $1.55 per bushel. Evidence of this is to be found in the 1947 Hansard at page 787. The then minister of trade and commerce had this to say:
Another question asked by the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. McCuaig) was, did the government sell Canadian wheat to forty-two countries outside the United Kingdom at $1.55 a bushel, or around 45 cents a bushel under world prices? The answer is that on September 19, 1945, the government instructed the Canadian wheat board to sell wheat for export at prices not exceeding $1.55
Canadian Wheat Board Act a bushel basis in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver. This instruction was of a temporary nature and was lifted on July 31, 1946. It covered a critical overseas position in the period following liberation.
Further down he has this to say:
This temporary policy was accompanied by a commitment on the part of the government "to ensure that producers will not, at any time up to July 31, 1950, receive less than $1 per bushel" for No. 1 Northern wheat, basis in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver. As the house now well knows, we have been able to do very much better than the basis outlined on September 19, 1945.
The idea seems to be held by a good many people that Britain somehow or other must have come on bended knees and pleaded with Canada to give her special consideration under which she would be able to obtain wheat for $1.55 per bushel. These quotations which I have given clearly prove that any such assumption concerning Britain is fallacious. That matter too has an important bearing on the question of the moral responsibility of Britain. Certainly, Britain had nothing to do with forming the wheat policy which was laid down, and which was being implemented by Canada. This order in council continues in force, as the quotation indicates, until July 31, 1946.
The wheat agreement now under discussion was signed on July 24, 1946, while that order in council was yet in force. Consequently, it can be said that the wheat agreement now under discussion was entered into by virtue of the order in council of September 19, 1945. The agreement was signed by James A. MacKinnon for Canada and P. A. Clutterbuck for Britain; and the treaty was in force immediately.
Before we go on with the next aspect of this question may I say this: Can anyone up to this stage find the slightest hint of any moral responsibility on Britain? Emphatically no!
Of this treaty the now much-disputed "have regard to" clause was article 2 (b) which, for the sake of the record, I propose to read once more. Article 2 (b) of the agreement between Canada and the United Kingdom for the purchase of Canadian wheat reads as follows:
(b) The actual prices to be paid for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1948-49 shall be negotiated and settled between the United Kingdom government and the Canadian government not later than the 31st December, 1947, and prices for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1949-50 shall be negotiated and settled not later than the 31st December, 1948. In determining the prices for these two crop years, 1948-49 and 1949-50, the United Kingdom government will have regard to any difference between the prices paid under this agreement in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years and the world prices for wheat in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years.

Those who argue that Britain has some moral responsibility usually point to this clause to begin their discussion. Any blame on Britain, if there be any blame, must have grown out of the last sentence of article 2 (b). Let us look at it again. I read the last sentence once more:
In determining the prices for these two crop years,
1948-	49 and 1949-50, the United Kingdom government will have regard to any difference between the prices paid under this agreement in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years and the world prices for wheat in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years.
"These two years" were 1948-49 and 194950. So it states. When written into the agreement, what was the significance of this so-called "have regard to" clause? I can remember quite well, Mr. Speaker, going throughout my constituency during the time when farmers were selling their wheat at $1.55 and having farmers quite anxiously ask me if I thought there was any chance that the price of wheat would go up during the next two years or if I did not fear that possibly the price of wheat would go down. I pointed to the "have regard to" clause and
I	said that the British people had always kept their word; that I believed that the "have regard to" clause was written into the agreement with the express purpose of providing protection against a fall in price of their product; that I believed that if there was any justification whatsoever, the British would negotiate the price upward from $1.55 so that we might expect such a price, we will say, as $1.75 or $1.80 next year. To me at the time this clause was a sort of guarantee that the price for wheat in 1948-49 and in
1949-	50 would be more than $1.55 per bushel if the prices paid for Canadian wheat by nations other than Britain were found to be sufficiently higher than $1.55 per bushel to justify an increase over $1.55 per bushel for Canadian wheat. So it worked out. The price of Canadian wheat to countries other than Britain in 1946-47 and 1947-48-in other words, the price of what was then called class II wheat-proved to be considerably higher than the $1.55 per bushel that Britain had agreed to pay and did pay.
Very well then. Recognizing this fact, Britain at the appropriate time "had regard to" that fact and agreed to pay $2 a bushel for her wheat in 1948-49. True to her agreement she did pay $2 per bushel in 1948-49. If that was not having respect for the "have regard to" clause, then I will challenge anybody in the house or in the country to prove that it was not.
Again at the appropriate time for making agreement to pay for 1949-50 wheat, once more Britain "had regard to" prices of class
II	wheat in 1946-49. She also had regard

to the probable price of class II wheat in the 1949-50 year. Having such regard, she agreed to pay $2 a bushel for the year 194950. Then, true to her agreement once more, she paid that price and took the full amount of wheat she had agreed to pay for and receive, notwithstanding the fact that the international wheat agreement arrived at meanwhile had fixed the price of class II wheat at $1.80. Once more you have an example of the application of the "have regard to" clause.
I have not heard anyone refer to that clause to give Britain any credit at all-a most astonishing thing. How can anyone show that Britain's behaviour in respect of her obligations up to that time had been less than fully moral? She did what she said she would do. She said in the agreement that she would have regard to the prices which had prevailed during the 1946-47 period, during the first two years, when she came to negotiate the prices for the next two years. She negotiated the prices for the next two years forty-five cents above what they were the first two years, thereby showing that she had regard. I believe that the people who are so anxious to attach moral turpitude-I do not know whether you would call it that; I suppose that is a little bit too strong an expression-or moral culpability to Britain by reason of the "have regard to" clause had better reconsider the whole matter in the light of what I have just said.
We now come to consider two pronouncements of responsible British statesmen. As I go around in the corridors and among the members I hear much reference to these two statements. The first of these was a statement by Right Hon. John Strachey. This gentleman, the British food minister, speaking before the Canadian Club at Winnipeg on February 26, 1947, quoted the latter part of clause 2 (b), the so-called "have regard to" clause, and then said:
Now these words mean neither more nor less than they say. They mean that the fact that we have bought our wheat from you this year below world prices-and that we may do so again next year-will be one of the factors in negotiating the actual prices to be paid in the third and fourth years. I and my government, and I am quite sure that this applies also to the Canadian government, would resist any attempt to add to or to subtract from this clear and definite statement as written into paragraph two subsection (b) of the wheat agreement.
Let us examine these words to see whether we can get from them the moral turpitude which some people feel inclined to impute to Britain. The words that have given rise to contention are those in the first two sentences; and it is not easy to see how words could be simpler or clearer in their meaning. They set forth exactly what the

British had agreed to do in clause 2 (b) of the agreement. They set forth precisely the course of procedure the British representatives adopted, together with the Canadian representatives, in determining that the price of $2 per bushel should be paid in each of the last two years, an increase of 45 cents a bushel over the first two years. How can anyone attach any blame to Britain on account of that speech or that remark? And I ask, how could any other interpretation have been justifiably placed upon those words than the interpretation I have given?
The second statement is that of Sir Stafford Cripps, chancellor of the British exchequer. On February 23, 1947, in an interview given to the Canadian Press in London, that statesman said:
As regards wheat we shall continue to depend on Canada for the greater part of our supplies. The four-year contract negotiated in 1946 will expire in 1950 and we have recently agreed upon a price of $2 a bushel for the 1949-50 season. We think there is every possibility of the world price falling below the $2 level before the end of the contract either because of the general improvement in the supply position or as a condition of any international wheat agreement which may be concluded in the near future. If this should be the case, the Canadian farmer will enjoy a favoured position by virtue of the fixed price on which we have agreed. This might prove to be a fair compensation for the earlier years when he was selling us wheat at below the world price; it depends, of course, upon how far prices actually fall. But in any case we have agreed to discuss this matter further with the Canadian government some time toward the end of 1950.
What do we gather from this pronouncement? This remark also has given rise to much contention. Let us consider the three most contentious sentences in the statement. The first, I submit, is this:
If this should be the case, the Canadian farmer will enjoy a favoured position by virtue of the fixed price on which we have agreed.
The British indicate no desire, because of the fixed world price, to ask any reduction from the $2 they agreed to pay for the third and fourth years of the contract. The British agreed to pay $2, and they paid it. There was no breach of honour there. I defy anyone, I do not care who he is, to show any breach of moral obligation in respect of that sentence.
Now let us take the second sentence which has given rise to discussion:
This might prove to be a fair compensation for the earlier years when he was selling us wheat at below the world price; it depends, of course, upon how far prices actually fall.
"Fair compensation" is the expression upon which one must concentrate attention. When Canada laid down her policy under P.C. 6122 in September, 1945, she had no thought of "compensation" from Britain. This is an
Canadian Wheat Board Act exceedingly important matter. When Canada negotiated the trade agreement she had no thought whatever of any compensation from Britain. Neither did the hon. members of this house; neither did the people throughout the country at that time. So when Sir Stafford Cripps spoke of a fair compensation I say he was exceedingly generous. The importance which has been attached to that expression by critics obviously is altogether unwarranted.
Look again at the order in council I have already read. What is more, look once again at the words of Mr. MacKinnon, which I have quoted, as evidence of the truth of my statement when I declared that Canada had no thought whatsoever of any compensation. Canada sold grain to probably forty or forty-five different nations other than Britain at $1.55 a bushel. We have not heard anyone suggest that any one of those be asked to make some compensation for the cheap grain they enjoyed. Why should we fix on Britain?
The farmer was entitled to substantial compensation-at least 25 cents per bushel. But the British had no responsibility in the matter, legally or morally.
Then the third sentence in the statement which has caused discussion is:
But in any case we have agreed to discuss this matter further with the Canadian government some time toward the middle of 1950.
The British did discuss this matter further, which was all they promised to do. In fact the British evidently asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to discuss the matter. As evidence of that I quote an interjection by the minister during the remarks of the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) at page 1115 of Hansard for March 9: After the arrangements were made for the sale of the 1950 wheat crop, I was asked to discuss the settlement of the four-year wheat agreement. They told me their views, and I gave the views of the Canadian government as I understood them. I brought back a message to the Canadian government.
Not only did the British discuss the matter; they sought an opportunity to discuss it, and thereby certainly discharged every vestige of responsibility, legally, morally or otherwise, which might have been suggested by the statement of Sir Stafford Cripps. So in what conceivable respect can it be shown that Britain in any degree failed to carry out her moral obligation arising from the words of Sir Stafford Cripps?

That this bill be not now read a second time, but that further consideration thereof be deferred until this house has had an opportunity to record its opinion on the government's announced decision with respect to the final settlement of the five-year wheat pool, and on the government's mishandling of the sale of wheat and other grains covered by the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
The word "mishandling", Mr. Speaker, is the chief reason why I rise to say a few words this evening. I should first like to advise the previous speaker that all producer organizations in western Canada requested the present wheat board set-up for the marketing of our grain.
There have been a lot of words spoken and written about a so-called loss on the five-year pool and the four-year contract with Britain. These writers and orators close their mind to the past, forget world conditions and only quote the present swing of world inflation. Have we not memories or do we close our minds to the past in order to forget what happened in the open market? Britain, the largest buyer of our wheat, now buys in bulk. Are we in a position to sell her in small lots or are we to allow a combination of traders to get together to pool their purchases to make this bulk delivery? The producers can remember when the wheat board was thrown over in 1920 following world war I, and these few speculative traders had a chance to show their stuff. Wheat hit a high of $2.85 a bushel early in September, 1920, when the wheat began to pour on the market, and by December, 1923, it was carried to the low average of 93-J cents. We all know the picture of conditions that followed.
Compare that situation with what occurred during the five years after world war II. Stabilization was secured. Could this speculative market operate today? Following the outbreak of war, and before it ended, the wheat board had to carry as high as 600 million bushels. Could speculators operate when importing countries could only purchase by loans or gifts? The government had to make these loans and gifts. Under the board the price was stabilized, and for the first time in our history the farmer knew the minimum price when he seeded. Being a free man in a free democracy, he could manage his business with a degree of confidence.
Before the frost hit the wheat board was faced with a most difficult marketing problem. It would have had to find consumers for a 500 million bushel wheat crop. Those consumers would have to have sufficient dollars with which to buy the wheat, and be prepared to pay enough for it to justify the original $1.40 initial payment. The frost eased
Canadian Wheat Board Act that selling problem but handed the board a far more difficult one, that of finding buyers for over 100 million bushels of wheat good only for feeding to livestock. The same rains that produced the bumper wheat crop gave the west an abundance of pasture and feeds. That fact alone has made feed wheat of less value than would otherwise have been the case. In order to find any kind of market for it, it must be priced at a point where it can be utilized as stock feed. This, then, is a real distress crop; an embarrassment to the producers, the wheat board, and the economy of the country.
To take the position that the wheat board should have set an artificially high price for feed wheat to compensate farmers for the terrible loss they suffered from frost is utterly illogical. The wheat board has but one function, to market the farmers' grain for the best possible price and to return to the farmers the net proceeds of the crop. The wheat board exists because the farmers of the west have become convinced that over the long term it provides price stability unknown under the boom and bust futures market system. All the farmers of the west have ever wanted, and ever hoped to get, was a fair average price for their wheat, not $3 one year and 35 cents the next. Before the wheat board, wheat might have been priced at $1.50 before the farmer planted it; $1.75 in July before harvest, and $1 when they hauled their crop to the elevator. When the price was high they had nothing to sell. When they had wheat to sell the price was often ruinous.
If the farmers of the west can get the average of what our overseas customers are prepared to pay for our wheat, that is all most producers have ever wanted. They have only wanted a system without the wild speculative fluctuations that were part and parcel of the futures market system. If the wheat board is to be the target for unreasoned abuse every time an initial price is set, and every time any other problem of marketing arises, the days of the board are surely numbered. It cannot stand much more of the kind of friendship it has been getting this past year.
Before sitting down, Mr. Speaker, I think I am going to put my finger on the crux of the whole system of marketing wheat in the world. I am taking in a lot of territory, but I believe I am going to give some information now that I have never heard in this house before. Regardless of what has been said by many of the grain trade representatives or any hon. member in this house, I contend that not one of them has mentioned the one thing which I consider has completely

Canadian Wheat Board Act changed the picture in so far as wheat marketing is concerned for all exporting countries in the world. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that was the closing of the Liverpool corn or grain exchange. I contend, sir, that there is no similar market in any country in the world today. The action of the British government in 1940 revolutionized the selling of wheat. In the face of that fact, I want to commend this government and the wheat board for their policy in disposing of our exportable wheat, which means so much to the grain producers and to the Canadian economy.
Now, Mr. Speaker, prior to the closing of the Liverpool grain exchange, when we looked at the marketing page of any newspaper in any country in the world to ascertain the price of wheat, what did we see? The first market that was mentioned in any column in any newspaper was Liverpool. What do we see today? We do not see Liverpool mentioned any longer. I contend that Chicago and Winnipeg have not taken the place of the Liverpool corn or grain exchange. These markets are in exporting countries and not in an importing country such as England is. Great Britain probably was, and is today, the greatest importer of wheat of any country in the world.

The document I hold in my hand reads as follows:
United Kingdom-Canadian Wheat Talks May 1950
Agreed Record of a Meeting in the Foreign Secretary's Room in the House of Commons at 2.30 p.m. on Monday 22nd May 1950
Present:
United Kingdom: Chancellor of the Exchequer (in the Chair); Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations; Minister of State for Economic Affairs; Minister of Food; Sir Percivale Liesching; Sir Henry Wilson Smith; Sir Frank Lee; Mr. A. E. Feavearyear.
Canada: Mr. C. D. Howe; Mr. L. B. Pearson; Mr. L.	D. Wilgress; Mr. Norman A. Robertson; Mr. M.	W. Mackenzie; Mr. G. A. Mclvor.
Secretary: Mr. F. Hollins.
1.	The meeting considered the following three questions in the light of the discussions that had taken place since Friday, 19th May:
(a)	The quantity of wheat to be bought by the United Kingdom from Canada in the crop year 1950/51.
(b)	The proportion of the quantity at (a) which the United Kingdom would take in the form of flour.
(c)	The final settlement of any question still outstanding under clause 2 (b) (the "have regard to" clause) of the United Kingdom/Canada contract of 1946.
2.	The conclusions reached on these three subjects were as follows:
(a)	The United Kingdom and Canadian governments would both make agreed announcements on the results of the conversations in the terms of the statement at Annex A. The United Kingdom government would have no objection to Mr. Howe stating publicly on his return to Canada, if he considered it desirable, that he thought it reasonable to assume that in 1950/51 Canada would be able to sell to the United Kingdom at competitive international wheat agreement prices somewhere between 100-120 million bushels of wheat. This quantity would include the carry-over of 12-5 million bushels bought under the terms of the four-year contract. The Chancellor of the Exchequer would also be prepared to make a public statement to the effect that the United Kingdom government hoped that they would be able to meet their requirements for dollar wheat from their traditional market in Canada within the international wheat agreement, and that this would be possible provided that such wheat could be purchased on terms as to price, quality and position not less favourable than those obtained by any other buyer in the dollar market whether in the United States of America or in Canada.

(b)	As part of its purchases of Canadian wheat in the crop year 1950/51 the United Kingdom would agree to take 300,000 tons of flour, provided that it could be purchased on terms not less favourable as to price and quality than those obtained by any other buyer of flour in the dollar market, whether in the United States of America or Canada. The United Kingdom representatives made it clear that the purchase of 300,000 tons in 1950/51 would be without prejudice to a possible lower scale of purchase in 1951/52.
Now comes clause (c) to which I wish to direct particular attention'*.
(c)	The United Kingdom was anxious not to be represented as having given assurances regarding wheat purchases in 1950/51 in return for the waiver of a claim by Canada under the "have regard to" clause. The United Kingdom expected to make large purchases of wheat from Canada in any event. Nevertheless, in the context of these discussions, the United Kingdom representatives felt that it would be reasonable that all obligations under the "have regard to" clause might be considered to have been taken care of. Mr. Howe said that this was a matter which could only be settled by the Canadian cabinet on his return.
Instead of reading the next paragraph, I think perhaps I should read the message that was sent from Canada after the Canadian cabinet had considered this minute. The Minister of Agriculture told us that the action under the minute was taken unanimously. May I just point out that there had been a lapse of eight days from the time the conference was held in London until the message was sent to Britain on May 30. During those eight days there was no protest from the Canadian government with respect to the "have regard to" clause and no suggestion that further negotiations should be held to modify the conclusion that had been reached and which is to be found in this return. On May 30, 1950, this message was sent to the Chancellor of the Exchequer. I had better read the letter which accompanies it. It is as follows:
Ottawa, May 30, 1950
Dear Sir Alexander:
Regarding the recent wheat talks in London, I am sending you, herewith, a message for the Chancellor of the Exchequer from the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I would be grateful if this could be sent off to London at once.
Yours sincerely,
A. D. P. Heeney
Sir Alexander Clutterbuck,
High Commissioner for the United Kingdom, Earnscliffe,
Ottawa.
The message is as follows:
Ottawa, May 30, 1950
Following for the Chancellor of the Exchequer from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, begins:
I have reported to my colleagues in the Cabinet on our recent wheat talks in London, and wish to let you know that they are in accord with the conclusions recorded in paragraph 2 (a), (b) and
Canadian Wheat Board Act (c) of the agreed record of the meeting which we held in the Foreign Secretary's room in the House of Commons on Monday, May 22nd.
In the circumstances, I should very much like to make public the agreed statement today, May 30th, if possible at 3.00 p.m. Ottawa time.
The agreed statement-and I do not think I need to put it on the record again-was annex A of this agreement. If we look at the statement that was agreed upon, identified as annex A, we find that after it was read to this house on May 30 last the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) this question:
May I ask the minister if at this conference a basis of settlement under the "have regard to" clause was discussed?
He went on to speak of the losses he believed had been sustained; and the answer of the minister was:
I understand the wheat board act will be discussed later in the session, and I do not care to amplify this statement at the moment.
That was the very day the message was sent to Britain stating that the government of Canada was in accord with the view in clause (c) of paragraph 2 of this agreement. The matter was settled by that exchange. It was settled first of all tentatively, as it were, in London. It could not be settled definitely because the Minister of Trade and Commerce and his colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) had not the authority. But when they got back the cabinet agreed, and authorized the minister to so notify the chancellor of the exchequer. So there is no possibility whatever of saying anything other than that an agreement and settlement of this matter was made. The other evening someone saw fit to criticize me because I had not been in touch with the British government. Well, of course it is not my place or my prerogative to get in touch with the British government on a matter under negotiation between our two governments. On the other hand, how could any member of this house have got in touch with the British government when, that agreement having been made on May 30, the Minister of Trade and Commerce answered the hon. member for Souris as he did? In other words none of us knew that this matter had been settled. I say there has been a deplorable lack of frankness in this connection; and the later attempts to re-open discussions could not possibly have succeeded because of the firm agreement that had been made in the exchange of the minute and the message of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the chancellor on May 30, 1950.
I do not know what this reference is to a waiver, but evidently there was consider-

Does my hon. friend think it was done? Does he think the British government would send out an agreed minute if they did not wish to be represented as accepting a waiver? Does he think they really did accept a waiver and then did not want to be represented as having done so?

I repeat that the essence of the agreement is that in return for selling wheat at $1.55 during the first two years of the agreement, Canadian farmers get the protection of minimum floor prices of $1.25 and $1 in the third and fourth years. In other words if there was a difference of opinion regarding this "have regard to" clause as between the Canadian and British governments, apparently the understanding of Mr. Strachey at that time was something which incidentally I did not understand at the time-
Will the hon. member permit me a question?
No.
Sit down.
What is the date of that?

I want to finish what I am
saying. Mr. Strachey's idea of this agreement, to some extent, was a sort of insurance policy that he was offering. When they arrived back they placed that minute containing the settlement proposed by the British government before the cabinet, and we are told that the cabinet unanimously gave the Minister of Trade and Commerce the right to send a message saying:
I have reported to my colleagues in the cabinet on our recent wheat talks in London, and wish to let you know that they are in accord with the conclusions recorded in paragraph 2 (a), (b) and (c) of the agreed record of the meeting which we held in the foreign secretary's room in the House of Commons on Monday, May 22nd.

I rise on a point of privilege. I have as much right in this house as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) or anybody else, and I would like to know the date of the document he is reading from.

I have given it. This is an agreed minute tabled by the Prime Minister tonight, the minute of the meeting held in London on May 22, 1950; and the message I have just read was sent by the secretary of the Privy Council of Canada, Mr. A. D. P. Heeney, after the cabinet meeting. It is dated May 30, 1950, in other words months before the "have regard to" clause was raised again in any way, either by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) or by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). During that week-during the week between the London meeting and the Ottawa meeting-there was no attempt on the part of the cabinet or, so far as we know, any member of the cabinet, to say to the government of Great Britain, "We are not satisfied with this deal; we would like to negotiate further."
On the contrary, they said, "We accept this agreement and we authorize the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to send a message" in the words I have just read. During that week there was no attempt to reopen the matter for Canadian farmers. No

attempt was made to call in representatives of the producers of this country, no attempt to call in the advisory committee of the wheat board-nothing of that kind. The matter was firmly and finally signed, sealed and delivered.
A sell-out.

Anyone who goes across
this country today and says that after this there was either a legal or moral obligation left over is wilfully and deliberately deceiving the people of Canada-and no peradven-ture about it. It is clear as crystal.
Making a lot of noise.
The hon. member says I am making a lot of noise tonight.
Not you, the crew behind you.

What I am saying, even if I did say it in a loud voice, is that there is no misunderstanding as to what this document means. And I say to hon. members on all sides of the house that they should cease- cease-misrepresenting this matter, anywhere.
The British government under this agreement says, "We are going to take large quantities of wheat from Canada"-100 million to 120 million bushels. Well, before the war, you know, the very best we could do in our sales of wheat to Britain was an average of about, I think, 90 million bushels a year. We have a market now in the United Kingdom for more.
Do you think that any people or any government will receive kindly some of the unjustifiable and unjustified criticism that has been thrown across the floor of this house during the last week or so? I say this trade is vital-and I do not care what government is in power in Great Britain, or what its political complexion may be, that government will fulfil an agreement which has been entered into.
Apparently the Canadian government agreed, in the message which was sent by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to London on May 30-
May I ask a question?
Just a moment; I will let you in a moment-on May 30, that the agreement had been fulfilled. I will take the hon. member's question now.
Why is the waiver sentence in there? Why did they want the waiver in it?

They did not. There is no suggestion of that-in fact, quite the con-B0709-84
Canadian Wheat Board Act trary. It is quite the contrary. What did they say regarding waiver? They say:
The United Kingdom government was anxious not to be represented as having given assurances regarding wheat purchases in 1950-51 in return for the waiver of a claim by Canada under the "have regard to" clause. The United Kingdom expected to make large purchases of wheat from Canada in any event.
What they said was:	We do not care
whether you hold us to something that you think you can read into the wheat agreement, or not. We are not going to do other than purchase a large quantity of wheat from Canada in 1950-51. That is what it means and what it says.

Canadian Wheat Board Act undertaking to purchase wheat. And there was an agreed statement to be made public, which was not to be made public until after he had reported to his colleagues in Canada, and had communicated an answer to them.

The conclusion of paragraph (c) is that this could only be settled by the Canadian cabinet, upon his return. But they did not say that definitely. They say that "It would be reasonable that all obligations under the 'have regard to' clause"-and so on. Do they not leave the way open for further negotiations, if the government thought of applying for further negotiations?

I admitted to him that perhaps he might say to me that I had no right to talk about the "have regard to" clause at that time in view of the minute of May and the answer that had been made. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we will give priority to wheat. The second item will be Bill No. 79, an act respecting Indians, and then Bill No. 130 an act to amend the Export and Import Permits Act. If we have time we will then take up a small bill or resolution.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, March 16, 1951
